n: The Philistines gather their army in Judah's territory, between Shochoh and Azekah, in the foothills west of Bethlehem. They are pushing into Israel's land.

f.g: A town in the lowland hills of Judah overlooking the Elah valley.

n: Saul and Israel camp in the valley of Elah and line up for battle.

f.g: “Valley of the terebinth (oak) tree,” a broad valley that was a natural route into Judah's hill country.

n: The two armies face each other from hills on opposite sides of the valley, with the valley between. Neither side wants to attack downhill and climb the other slope.
A champion comes out from the Philistine camp: Goliath of Gath, about nine and a half feet tall. Ancient armies sometimes settled battles through single combat between champions.

f.g: A cubit is about 18 inches and a span about 9, so roughly 9 feet 9 inches. Some ancient manuscripts and Josephus read four cubits and a span, about 6 feet 9 inches.

n: He wears a bronze helmet and scale armor weighing about 125 pounds — a walking fortress.

f.g: armor made of overlapping bronze scales

n: Bronze shin guards protect his legs, and a bronze javelin hangs between his shoulders.

f.g: Here probably a javelin, or possibly a small shield.

n: His spear shaft is as thick as a weaver's beam, with an iron head weighing about fifteen pounds. A shield-bearer walks ahead of him.

f.g: A thick wooden rod on a loom; it may also describe a spear with a loop and cord for throwing.

n: Goliath shouts a challenge: why fight a full battle? Pick one man to come and fight me.
He proposes winner-take-all: whichever champion wins, his nation will rule the other.
Goliath openly defies — mocks and taunts — Israel's armies, and with them, Israel's God.
Saul and all Israel are terrified. Saul, the tall king chosen to fight Israel's battles, has no answer.
The narrator reintroduces David as the son of Jesse of Bethlehem, who had eight sons and was elderly by this time.

f.g: from the clan of Ephrath, the Bethlehem area

n: Jesse's three eldest sons — Eliab, Abinadab, and Shammah — have joined Saul's army.
David is the youngest; only the three oldest went to war.
David goes back and forth between serving Saul and tending his father's sheep at Bethlehem. He was faithful in small duties.
For forty days Goliath comes out morning and evening to repeat his challenge. Forty is often a number of testing in scripture.
Jesse sends David with supplies for his brothers: roasted grain and ten loaves of bread. Soldiers often depended on their families for food.
David is also to bring cheeses to his brothers' commander, check on his brothers, and bring back some token that they are well.

f.g: bring back a token or proof of their welfare

n: Saul and the army are still in the valley of Elah, facing the Philistines.
David rises early, leaves the sheep with a keeper, and arrives at camp just as the army is going out to battle positions shouting the war cry.

f.g: the camp's barricade or circle of wagons

n: Both armies are drawn up in battle lines, facing each other.
David leaves his supplies with the baggage keeper and runs to the battle line to greet his brothers.
While he talks with them, Goliath comes out and repeats his challenge, and David hears it for the first time.
At the sight of Goliath, all the Israelite soldiers flee in terror.
The soldiers talk about the king's reward for anyone who kills Goliath: great wealth, marriage to the king's daughter, and freedom from taxes for his family.

f.g: exempt his family from taxes and royal service

n: David asks about the reward, but his real concern shows: who is this pagan to defy the armies of the living God? David sees the situation spiritually while others see only the giant.
The soldiers repeat to David what the king will do for whoever kills Goliath.
Eliab angrily accuses David of pride and wicked motives, mocking his “few sheep.” The brother whom Samuel first thought chosen now resents the one God chose.
David answers, “What have I done now? Can't I even ask a question?” He doesn't let his brother's anger stop him.

f.g: Probably “It was only a question” or “Isn't there good reason?”

n: David turns to someone else, asks the same thing, and gets the same answer.
David's words reach Saul, who sends for him.
David encourages the king: no one should lose heart because of this Philistine — I will go and fight him.
Saul objects that David is only a youth, while Goliath has been a warrior since his own youth.

f.g: a young man, perhaps a teenager

n: David explains his experience: as a shepherd he faced lions and bears that attacked the flock.
He went after the predator, rescued the lamb from its mouth, and when it turned on him, seized it and killed it. A good shepherd risks his life for the sheep.

f.w: delivered it out of his mouth

f.g: the hair on its jaw or mane

n: David has killed both lion and bear, and this Philistine will be like them, because he has insulted the armies of the living God.
David gives the credit to God: the Lord who saved him from lion and bear will save him from this Philistine. His courage rests on past experiences with God's help. Saul blesses him.
Saul dresses David in his own armor, bronze helmet, and coat of mail — trying to fight the Lord's battle with the king's methods.
David tries walking in the armor but isn't used to it. He takes it off. He will face Goliath with what he knows and with faith in God.
David takes his staff, chooses five smooth stones from the stream, puts them in his shepherd's bag, and approaches with his sling. Simple tools in faithful hands.

f.g: A strap with a pouch, swung to hurl stones with great speed and accuracy; slingers were a real part of ancient armies.

n: Goliath advances toward David, his shield-bearer in front.
Goliath looks David over and is insulted — just a ruddy, good-looking boy. Like Samuel earlier, he judges by appearance.
“Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?” Goliath mocks and curses David by his gods. The contest becomes a clash between gods.
Goliath threatens to feed David's body to birds and wild animals — the worst dishonor in that culture.
David's reply is the heart of the story: you come with sword, spear, and shield; I come in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God you have defied.

f.w: in the name of the LORD of hosts

n: David boldly predicts victory, and gives its purpose: so all the earth will know there is a God in Israel. The battle is about God's glory, not David's fame.

f.w: that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel

n: Everyone will learn that the Lord does not save by sword and spear, for the battle belongs to the Lord.
As Goliath approaches, David doesn't wait — he runs toward the battle line to meet him. Faith moves forward.
David slings a stone that strikes Goliath in the forehead and sinks in, and the giant falls face down — like Dagon falling before the ark.
The narrator emphasizes that David won with just a sling and a stone, without a sword. God's power, not weapons, gave the victory.
David runs over, takes Goliath's own sword, kills him, and cuts off his head. The Philistines see their champion fall and flee.
Israel's army, suddenly brave, raises the war cry and chases the Philistines back to Gath and Ekron. Wounded Philistines fall all along the road.

f.g: A town in the Shephelah (foothills), meaning “two gates.”

n: Returning from the chase, the Israelites plunder the Philistine camp.
David brings Goliath's head to Jerusalem — possibly written in hindsight, since Jerusalem was not yet Israelite — and keeps the armor in his tent.

f.g: Jerusalem was still held by the Jebusites until David captured it later.

n: Watching David go out, Saul asks Abner whose son the young man is. Abner doesn't know. Since Saul knew David as a musician, he may have meant which family he came from, given the promised reward.

f.g: Saul needed to know the family whose house he had promised to free from taxes (v. 25).

n: Saul tells Abner to find out who the young man's father is.
When David returns, Abner brings him to Saul, still holding Goliath's head.
Saul asks David whose son he is, and David humbly answers: the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem. The shepherd boy has entered the national stage.
